newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic under pressure from opposition, Montenegro.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic under pressure from opposition, Montenegro.

text.p: Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic's rule came under pressure on Friday when he lost control of Belgrade city council and Montenegro dealt a potentially fatal blow to his hopes of retaining power in Yugoslavia.

On the day an opposition coalition took the reigns of power in Serbia's capital city, ending 50 years of socialist rule, Montenegrin Prime Minister Mile Djukanovic warned Milosevic he would not get the Montenegrin votes he needs to switch from the Serbian to the Yugoslav presidency this year.
Djukanovic told the independent Belgrade weekly Vreme it would by "totally wrong" for Milosevic to stay and added:

"Milosevic's political thought is outdated; he lacks the ability to view things strategically and he is surrounded by the wrong people who keep him rather uninformed about the real scale of Serbia's and Yugoslavia's problems."

Montenegro, with a population of 550,000 compared with Serbia's 10.5 million, is the junior partner in the Yugoslav federation. But it is strongly placed to sabotage Milosevic's hopes of surviving more than three months of political turmoil in Serbia caused by his attempt to revoke opposition victories in local elections.
Barred by law from a third term as Serbian president, Milosevic planned to have himself elected Yugoslav president this year by the federal parliament.

Montenegrin votes would be essential both for his election and for constitutional changes to give the ceremonial federal office the wide-ranging executive powers Milosevic has wielded as Serbian president.
Serbian policies have kept Yugoslavia internationally isolated, refused entry to world diplomatic and financial bodies despite the lifting of U.N. sanctions.
Montenegro has threatened to try to reach separate agreements with the international community and if necessary to abandon the Yugoslav dinar and mint its own currency.
The election dispute added democratic reforms to the list of requirements the West is demanding from Belgrade in return for a gradual lifting of Yugoslavia's quarantine.

Co-leader of the Zajedno (Together) coalition of opposition parties, Zoran Djindjic, was elected mayor to loud applause in the chamber on Friday. He took over the chair of the assembly session within minutes of the vote and his coalition pledged to transform the workings of the old socialist council.

But another of the three co-leaders, bearded novelist Vuk Draskovic, said there was no reason to celebrate yet. "This is the beginning of hard, hard, very hard work and not the beginning of celebrations," he told Reuters.
"Until today we were in opposition. We had a right to dream, to make all kinds of promises. From today we're facing reality and we will be responsible for the life in this city."
Milosevic was forced to recognise Zajedno's victories after the demonstrations of up to half a million people attracted worldwide media attention and support from foreign governments.

Zajedno's breakthrough ignited a battle between Socialist Party hard-liners and pragmatists on ways to keep the opposition at bay ahead of Serbian presidential and parliamentary elections due by the end of 1997.
The pragmatists, with Montenegro's support, favoured an early compromise with Zajedno to appease the West and improve Yugoslavia's chances of winning aid to rebuild its economy.
The debilitating struggle, ending in defeat for the party, showed the rival wings to be evenly balanced with a weakened Milosevic unable to impose his will on either side.
